01
The problem
We're building interfaces that move. They don't always communicate.
Chapter 1 · The problem — Same screen, twice
Two interfaces. Same functionality.
Which one feels better — and more importantly, why?
Chapter 1 · The problem — Common habits
We have a movement problem
Animation added at the very end of development
Everything bounces, or everything fades
Copied from somewhere, without knowing why it worked there
One transition, reused for every interaction in the product
Just because something moves doesn't mean the experience is better.
Chapter 1 · The problem — The reframe
Motion is communication, not decoration.
What just happened?
Where did this come from?
What should I look at?
What happens next?
02
Motion is a language
Four jobs it does in an interface: feedback, continuity, attention, orientation.
Chapter 2 · Motion is a language — Feedback
Motion communicates feedback
Feedback is the interface saying “I heard you” before it has anything useful to report.
Perceived speed is mostly about the first frame. Anything that responds inside about 100 ms reads as instant, whatever the server does afterwards.
So a hundred milliseconds of local animation buys you a round trip you don't control.
idle → pressed → loading → success
Chapter 2 · Motion is a language — Continuity
Motion creates continuity
Every time a screen changes, the user has to work out how the new thing relates to the old one. Continuity does that work for them.
Keep the element alive across the change and the relationship is obvious. Destroy it and rebuild something similar, and they have to read the screen again from the top.
view-transition-name: card-42
Chapter 2 · Motion is a language — Attention
Motion directs attention
The eye goes to whatever moves, before any of the words get read. That makes movement the strongest signal in your interface.
It's also a fixed budget. Two things moving is half the signal each. Six things moving is no signal at all.
The amount needed is usually much smaller than people expect. A result appearing somewhere the user isn't looking needs a nudge, not a performance.
Chapter 2 · Motion is a language — Orientation
Motion provides orientation
Where a surface comes from tells people where it lives and how to get rid of it.
03
The craft
Timing, easing, choreography, transitions, and the small details.
Chapter 3 · The craft — Timing
How long should a change take?
How long a change should take depends on how far it travels, how big it is, and above all how often the person will sit through it.
Under 300 ms for most product UI. Marketing pages get more room, because nobody visits them forty times a day.
Chapter 3 · The craft — Easing
Four curves, four jobs
Nothing in the real world starts and stops at a constant speed, and each kind of change has a curve that suits it.
Easing also changes how fast something feels. Two dropdowns at an identical 300 ms read very differently depending on the curve. And the built-in curves are weaker than you want, so reach for custom ones.
Chapter 3 · The craft — Choreography
Not everything moves at once
A screen is a composition. The order things arrive in tells people what matters and where to start reading.
Lead with what they came for
Heading first, then the primary content, then the supporting detail.
Keep the gap small
40 to 60 ms between items. Past 80 it stops reading as one gesture and starts feeling like lag.
Know when to stop
Six cards is a sequence. Forty cards means the last one lands two seconds late.
Chapter 3 · The craft — Transitions
Don't just change states. Connect them.
A transition answers two questions at once: what changed, and how the new thing relates to the thing that was there before.
Chapter 3 · The craft — Micro-interactions
The details people feel
Polish is rarely one impressive thing. It is a dozen small moments that each took about an hour, and that nobody notices on their own.
Chapter 3 · The craft — Numbers
Small numbers worth stealing
scale(0.97)
Button press. Not 0.9, which looks squashed.
1–2%
Hover scale. scale-105 is almost always too much.
100–150ms
Hover duration. 300 is far too slow for this.
scale(0.9)
Lowest an entrance should start. Never from zero.
÷ 2
Exits run about half the entrance duration.
44px
Minimum hit target. Grow it with a pseudo-element.
2px blur
Bridges two states when a crossfade feels off.
child, not self
Move a child on hover, or the cursor leaves and it flickers.
Rules of thumb, not laws. If you're outside one of them, have a reason.
04
The instinct
Knowing when it's wrong, and how you get better at knowing.
Chapter 4 · The instinct — When to stop
When motion becomes noise
Nobody sets out to build this. It happens when four teams each add one defensible animation to the same screen over four quarters.
Chapter 4 · The instinct — States
Think in states, not effects
One button has six states. You already write all of them. Motion is the part of each change your user can see.
1
What changed?
2
Why did it change?
3
What should the user understand?
4
What movement says that?  Last question, not the first.
Chapter 4 · The instinct — Practice
Build your motion instincts
1
Observe
Catch yourself reacting to an interface you like.
2
Slow it down
Screen-record it and play it back at 0.25×.
3
Recreate
Rebuild it from scratch. The gap is the lesson.
4
Compare
Vary timing and easing. Put versions side by side.
5
Name it
Duration, curve, order, origin. Words beat feelings.
Tools
CSS transitions and keyframes · Web Animations API · Motion · DevTools animation inspector
Non-negotiables
Respect prefers-reduced-motion · animate transform and opacity · never cause layout shift

05
Iterating with AI
Trying more versions, and keeping the decision yourself.
Chapter 5 · Iterating with AI — Why it matters
Iteration just got cheap
The expensive part of motion was never writing the code. It was that trying a second version cost as much as the first — so most of us shipped the first.
Describe
State the behaviour, not the vibe.
Generate
Ask for three versions, not one.
Run
In the browser, at real size.
Compare
Side by side, then at 0.25×.
Decide
This part is still yours.
Chapter 5 · Iterating with AI — Prompting
Vocabulary is the interface
Gets you noise
“Make this animation feel smoother.”
Gets you what you pictured
“Slide the panel in from the right over 250ms, cubic-bezier(0,0,.2,1). Fade the backdrop in 50ms ahead of it. Transform and opacity only.”
Ask for three to five
Genuinely different directions, with a switcher to flip between them.
Make it explain
“Why that curve?” turns a generator into something you learn from.
Critique, don't restart
“Exit is too slow, halve it” beats regenerating from scratch.
And prototype with your worst content: long names, two-line titles, forty rows.

Write your own only where your product actually differs
Chapter 5 · Iterating with AI — Judgment
AI can generate movement.  You give it meaning.
Don't outsource your taste. Use AI to develop it.
It can
Write the code, suggest patterns, explore directions, prototype in minutes.
You decide
Whether it's appropriate, whether it communicates, whether it improves the experience.
06
The takeaway
What to do with all of this on Monday morning.
Chapter 6 · The takeaway — The checklist
Before you animate, ask
What am I trying to communicate?
Does this movement help the user?
Is the timing right for the distance?
How often will they see this?
Does it come from where it belongs?
Can it be interrupted?
Does it respect reduced motion?
Would this be better without it?
Chapter 6 · The takeaway — The one thing
Don't animate because you can.
Animate because it makes the experience better.
